content: The impact of food marketing on children has been studied extensively, with evidence suggesting significant effects on food preferences, choices, dietary intake, and product requests. However, the ability to assess the influence of specific marketing techniques, such as the use of promotional characters, toys, or celebrities, is limited due to the small number of studies available for each technique. For food choices and dietary intake, researchers attempted to evaluate the role of children’s mean age and BMI z-scores on the observed effects. However, this analysis was not feasible for food preferences due to insufficient data. Similarly, comparisons between high-income countries (HICs) and lowand middle-income countries (LMICs) were not possible. However, no statistical evidence was found to suggest that study design, type of marketing manipulation, or marketing medium significantly influenced the effect size. According to GRADE assessments, the certainty of evidence from RCTs and observational studies on food marketing’s effect on food preferences is very low. For food choices or intended choices, 37 studies (27 RCTs and 10 non-randomized experimental studies) provided evidence. Again, no statistical evidence indicated that study design, marketing manipulation type, marketing medium, risk of bias, or children’s mean age significantly moderated the effect size. Ten studies were excluded from pooled analysis due to insufficient data; six reported significant associations, two found no significant associations, one reported greater test item choice in the control condition (attributed to demographic targeting issues), and one described an association without statistical testing. GRADE assessments indicated moderate certainty evidence from RCTs that food marketing likely increases food choices, while observational evidence remains of very low certainty. The findings showed a significant effect of marketing on dietary intake compared to no or less powerful marketing. However, no statistical evidence suggested that study design, marketing manipulation type, marketing medium, risk of bias, children’s mean age, or BMI z-scores significantly influenced the effect size. Five studies lacked sufficient data for pooled analysis; three reported significant associations, and two found no significant associations. GRADE assessments indicated moderate certainty evidence from RCTs that food marketing slightly increases dietary intake, while observational evidence remains of very low certainty. For product requests or intended requests, six studies (five RCTs and one observational study) provided evidence. The findings indicated a significant effect of food marketing on product requests. GRADE assessments suggested moderate certainty evidence from RCTs that food marketing likely increases product requests, while observational evidence remains of very low certainty. Evidence on food purchasing or sales was limited, with five studies (one RCT and four non-randomized studies) providing data. Among these, one study reported a clear public health harm, one found unclear potential harm, two found no significant associations, and one reported a clear public health benefit (e.g., increased fruit dessert orders when promoted). GRADE assessments indicated very low certainty evidence from both RCTs and observational studies regarding the effect of food marketing on purchasing or sales. For dental caries/erosion, two observational studies provided evidence. One study reported a clear public health harm, while the other found no significant association. GRADE assessments indicated very low certainty observational evidence on the effect of food marketing on dental health outcomes. Policies to restrict food marketing to children were evaluated in 44 observational studies, assessing 14 policies implemented in 10 countries and one region. Most studies were conducted in HICs, with only one study from an LMIC (Mexico). Policies addressing television marketing and packaging were more effective than those targeting digital marketing. Government-led nutrient profile models were more likely to show beneficial effects than company-led models. Some studies highlighted the migration of marketing efforts to non-restricted spaces following policy implementation. For example, after the UK restricted high-fat, sugar, and salt (HFSS) food advertising on children’s channels, such advertising shifted to other times and channels viewed by children. In terms of contextual factors, 244 publications were reviewed. In HICs, overweight and obesity were generally perceived as serious health problems, particularly among women and individuals of lower socioeconomic status. In contrast, in many LMICs, overweight and obesity were often seen as indicators of good health, though this perception is changing in some countries. All identified modeling studies found that policies to protect children from harmful food marketing would be cost-effective or cost-saving. Finally, policies to protect children from harmful food marketing align with human rights standards, including the Convention on the Rights of the Child. Countries are obligated to take immediate action to protect children’s rights to health, adequate nutrition, and freedom from exploitation.
